items.title: A good morning-after read on the Cavs' it'd-be-unthinkable-if-it-wasn't-so-familiar meltdown, from @dannycunningham.bsky.social: theinsideshot.substack.com/p/game-night...
items.body_excerpt: A good morning-after read on the Cavs' it'd-be-unthinkable-if-it-wasn't-so-familiar meltdown, from @dannycunningham.bsky.social: theinsideshot.substack.com/p/game-night...

images.alt:
“It was completely our offense. Obviously the first half we’re making buckets. We’re getting our defense set. We’re getting back in transition,” Cavs head coach Kenny Atkinson said after the loss. “But, when you start those live ball turnovers, it’s especially a team that’s as fast as they are. So, I will not blame it on our defense. I think the culprit of this one was our offense. And, again, not being able to handle the pressure and physicality.”

Does that sound familiar?

That strategy is the same one that the Toronto Raptors turned to after losing the first two games to the Cavs in the first round of the playoffs last spring. That 2-0 series lead for Cleveland was erased before the Cavs won Game 7 at home. The Detroit Pistons used a similar strategy against the Cavs in the Eastern Conference Semifinals, another series that saw the Cavs win a Game 7.

It’s a new year, and a team that has enough differences that not everything is the same, but this very specific problem has already shown to be an issue on the opening night of the season. This loss for the Cavs needs to be a quick lesson that the blueprint to beating them is out and figuring out the way to solve it needs to be of the highest priority. Not every team in the NBA is capable of doing what the Sixers did against them on Thursday night, but the ones that are capable of winning the title are.

If the Cavs want to be included in that group, this is a problem that must be solved.
